Naturally, I would take that to be the case. Common sense would indicate that. Therefore, I say that that country would constitute the best market in the world for potatoes.

The hon. gentleman is
following his own preference. He is no doubt a large consumer of potatoes, and therefore he claims that the people of the United States are in the same catagory as himself. The people in the southern states do not use the sort of potato that is referred to in the statistics given by my hon. friend from Frontenac (Mr. Edwards), which referred to the kind of potato which is the favorite of the hon. member for Kings.
What is your particular favorite?

I, like my hon. friend,
prefer the Irish potato. That is where my
hon. friend gets wrong in his statistics.

I do not propose to refer to any of the rambling remarks about what they are doing in the United States per head and what they are not doing. I would like to hear from some of my Conservative friends from the province of Ne.w Brunswick as to how they feel on this question. But I would be particularly interested in hearing from the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Burrell) on the question of the embargo if he does not want, to talk on the question of the duty. I have tried to convince this committee that this is an important matter to the people of the Maritime provinces. I do not think that there is any person but will admit that. We all have to admit it and we are face to face with an exceedingly serious condition of affairs. It is no use for members on this side of the House or on the other to stand up and make general speeches on the theory of protection or free trade in so far as the farmers are concerned. We are discussing now a concrete case. There is no use in the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) quoting figures of the total production of the United States or the im-



poirtations from Europe or anything like that. We know in the Maritime provinces that the United States would offer a market for our potatoes if we could get them in there. Every farmer in New Brunswick knows that, every famier in Prince Edward Island knows that, every farmer in the Maritime provinces, be he Liberal or Conservative, knows it. Every man, no matter how he voted in 1911, knows it. They all want to get that market and they all realize that we cannot get into that market on account of this embargo. I want to come down to the real question at issue.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I understood.my hon. friend (Mr. Cairvell) to say that the United States would be influenced to remove the embargo if American potatoes were admitted into Canada free.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Let me ask my hon.^
friend one other question. What is the value to the American potato raiser of free entry into the Canadian market?-because I understood my hon. friend to say that that would be of no advantage to him. If that foe so, what is the value of the Canadian market to the United States on the strength of which they will be influenced to remove the existing embargo?

That is a fair question. In my judgment it amounted to nothing, but I think the American Government must have considered it as amounting to something or they would not have framed their tariff as they did. They refused free entry of Canadian potatoes into the United States because we would not allow free entry of American potatoes into Canada. Otherwise, they would not have left them at 10 per cent. They removed the duty as against other countries and let potatoes in free. The United States never could send a barrel of potatoes to any country in the world except Canada or Cuba. It would not be common sense to talk about sending potatoes from the United States to Europe; yet they have allowed European potatoes to come in free and they have imposed a duty of 10 per cent against Canadian potatoes, unless by our legislation we allow theirs to come in free of duty. I be ieve that this market does not amount to anything whatever to the United States producer because there is,

in my judgment, not the least possibility of potatoes coming into Canada from the United States, although in the summer months when we do not produce them they come from the southern or central states, where they mature much earlier than ours do in Canada. I may toe wrong in my conclusions, my arguments and my beliefs, but these are my conclusions, my arguments and my beliefs.
Now, I want to come back to the Minister of Agriculture. I have tried in the course of this argument to treat him fairly and any man except some of the backbenchers who heard what I said to the minister will admit that I treated him fairly. I have given him credit for sincerely trying to meet the situation. I believe the minister is honestly and earnestly trying to see a way out. I give him great credit for sending out this statement which we have had placed in our hands to-day with reference to the potato disease. I think it is going to be of great benefit to the potato raisers of Canada. I want to give the minister full credit for the attention which he has tried to give to this great question. But I think this committee is entitled to a statement from the minister as to what the condition is, as to what has been done and as to what, in his opinion, can be done. For fear a wrong impression should go abroad with reference to the action taken by the Department of Agriculture in regard to potato diseases, I wish to inform the House that in Prince Edward Island, in 1912, and again in 1913, there were two officials of the department travelling from house to house conducting investigations into this potato disease. Last year it was the intention of the Government to place a laboratory in the province, and to put in charge a bacteriologist of repute, but owing to some mishap he was unable to go there. However, I understand that this year the Government have secured the services of an official competent to take this matter in charge, and that the investigation will be further prosecuted in Prince Edward Island. I may say also that the provincial Department of Agriculture is acting in accord with the Dominion Department of Agriculture, and good work is being done. Rapid strides, are being made in agriculture in Prince Edward Island, as the hon. member for Kings (Mr. J. J. Hughes) knows. Had that hon. gentleman made inquiries at the department in Ottawa or at the department in Charlottetown, he would have found that these investigations were going on. I presume it is as a result of this investigation by the Department of Agriculture that this very interesting document, which we have received, has been issued. There is no doubt, as the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) has said, it is a move in the right direction, and one which probably should have been taken years ago, because it is well known that disease has existed in Canadian potatoes for many years.
Oh.no.

That is a fact. The
nature of the disease was not known, but that disease existed there can be no doubt. Canker did not exist in Canada and does not exist to-day, but powdery scab has existed in this country, and so long as no action is taken by the farmers themselves it will spread. It is up to the farmers whether they will let this disease spread or not.
It is a very serious statement for the hon. gentleman to make that potato disease has existed in Canada, for years.
I know what I am talking about.
On what authority does the hon. gentleman make that statement?

I make the statement because I know it is a fact. It is a fact that there is potato disease in Canada to-day, and the hon. member for Carleton admitted, that by Teason of that disease in his own province there was an embargo placed on potatoes going into the United States.

I must put the hon.
member right there. I was careful not to make any such statement. I said the United States Government claimed that, and claimed to have evidence of the fact, but I do not know whether that evidence is well-founded or not. I do not admit it and I said that I had grave doubt that disease did exist. I do not want my hon. friend (Mr. A. A. McLean) to put words in my mouth that I did not use. I do not believe that powdery scab existed up to two years ago, even if it exists now. If the Minister of Agriculture wants to give certain information he can give it, but it would perhaps not be wise to give all the facts in connection with the introduction of this powdery scab into Canada, if it be in Canada at all.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Carvell) cannot help admitting that he said that the United States Government were justified in placing an embargo on Canadian potatoes.

There again, my hon.
friend is misquoting me. I said the United States Government probably believed that they were justified.

That is a qualification
that the hon. gentleman makes now.
No it is not.

We all heard what, the
hon. gentleman said; we all heard him make the broad, plain statement that the United States Government were justified in putting an embargo on Canadian potatoes.

No, I did not. This is a matter of too much importance to let
pass.	I protest against the hon. gentleman attributing to me any such statement as that. I do not want him to repeat it again, because it is not true and he knows it is not true.

The same statement was
made 'by the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards), and the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) did not deny it.
I make it a practice in this House to not pay any attention whatever to anything said by the hon. member for Frontenac.

friend from Prince Edward Island (Mr. A.
A.	McLean) in the same category with the hon. member for Frontenac, and therefore when he makes a statement that is not in accordance with the facts I must call him to order.

Before six o'clock 1
addressed a question to the hon. member for Carleton to this effect: Does the hon. gentleman believe that the United States in putting an embargo against Canadian potatoes, were fair? and the hon. member for Carle-ton said: 'Yes.'
Certainly I did; that is a correct statement.

I have no doubt
that when we get ' Hansard ' to-morrow, we shall find that the statement I have made is correct.

speechtext: If a statement attributed to another member is denied by him, the word of the* hon. member must be accepted.

The hon. member for Carleton denies that he made that statement, and I suppose I must bow to your ruling, Mr. Chairman, and withdraw my statement. But, notwithstanding, the statement I made was that ' Hansard ' would show which one of us was right.
Take it back.
That is good enough; go on now.

The hon. gentleman said' further that he believed that probably scab existed in the state of Maine, and that the United States Government had appointed a commission to investigate the matter, and inspectors to inspect the potatoes shipped from that state. He said further, that if potatoes in Maine were found affected with scab, they were not allowed to be used for seed. There is no doubt that the hon. member for Carleton made the statement that the Maine potatoes were affected with powdery scab or some other infectious disease, because otherwise the United States Government, in whom he places great reliance in matters of this kind, would not have put an embargo on shipments of Maine potatoes for use as seed. We have this condition of affairs- an embargo put upon potatoes in the state of Maine and an embargo put upon potatoes from New Brunswick, or for that matter from the whole of Canada. It is the duty of the Government to investigate this matter, and I want to tell the hon. member for Kings (Mr. J. J. Hughes) that the Government has been investigating it for the last three or four years, that this investigation has been widespread, and that the Government is to-day in possession of very important information on the subject, which I have no doubt the Minister of Agriculture will give to the House.
I am not making a statement concerning things about which I know nothing. It is of so much importance to the people of my province that, no matter what it costs, the Government should take the matter up and investigate it properly. We were in the habit of selling our potatoes in the United States where we got very good prices for them. Sometimes we got a. higher price than at other times. Sometimes prices in Boston were higher than in New York and sometimes higher in St. John than in Boston. So far as Prince Edward Island was concerned, we had a home market at Sydney, Stellarton and other mining towns of the Maritime provinces. New Brunswick was not in a posi-

tion to produce enough potatoes to supply the markets of Nova Scotia. Sometimes the people of that province were not in a position to supply more potatoes than they could use themselves. Although New Brunswick is a large province, it has only about 40,000 acres under potatoes, which is a very small acreage in comparison with the acreage under potatoes in Prince Edward Island.

Would my hon. friend
tell me how long ago it was that New Brunswick was not in a position to supply more potatoes than it used itself?
In 19H we shipped half a million barrels of potatoes from my own county alone.
How was it, then, that potatoes came from the state of Maine to New Brunswick, and were sold in competition with potatoes of New Brunswick?
They did not come into the province of New Brunswick in 1911, and we have the records to show it.
Order, order.
Take it back.
Nothing is accomplished by this.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member for Queens, Prince Edward Island, has the floor. The hon. member for Carleton knows that he has no right to interrupt.

I do not suppose there is any gentleman who knows so much or who presumes to know so much as the hon. member for Carleton, but I think other hon. members have a right to give utterance to their views on questions under discussion. The hon. member for Carleton should not assume all the rights of every member or even of the members of his own party.
When my hon. friend is wrong-
Order.

When my hon. friend is wrong, I am going to put him right; make no mistake about that. I think my hon. friend and I get along very well. I presume that he wants to be fair. I have here a statement from the Customs Department of the imports and exports of potatoes for the last two years. My hon. friend can get these, and be absolutely accurate in his statements. Instead of
importing potatoes into New Brunswick in 1911, from my own county alone we exported close to half a million barrels, and the whole province of New Brunswick must have exported three-quarters of a million barrels in that year.
I have no doubt that, in his own mind, my hon. friend always thinks he is right,, and he will not concede to any other hon. member the privilege of being right.
Not when he is wrong.

According to the hon. member for Carleton, N.B., anything that any hon. member on this side of the House states is wrong; everything that he thinks is evil. It is very unfair to hon. members on this side of the House to be treated in that way by my hon. friend. He ought to make this concession, that every one of us is actuated with good intentions. We are here, not for party purposes; we are here, not for the best interest of Prince Edward Island or New Brunswick or Nova Scotia or Ontario or Quebec; we are here for the best interest of the whole of Canada. When my hon. friend takes upon himself to say, as he has in effect said, that the whole politics of this country should be guided by the quantity of potatoes going into the county of Carleton, I think he goes far afield. He should, as was done in the case of agricultural implements, upon which the duty was reduced, concede something to the manufacturers. He has conceded nothing to them. According to him, they should be turned down from one end of the *country to the other. What would be the-effect in the Maritime provinces to-day if the Nova Scotia Steel Works, the Dominion Steel Works, and the other great industries of that province were turned down, as would be the desire of the hon. member? Where would the markets be for the products of the farmer? There would be none. Since these manufactures have been established in the Maritime provinces under the tariff which we have now, the tariff of 1879, the farmers have become wealthy. To-day the farmers of Prince Edward Island, as a class, are the wealthiest people in Canada. We have the smallest province with the smallest population, but there is not another body of 95,000 people who have the same wealiM as we have. The people of Prince Edwam Island are all farmers, and have made their money through the farming industry -through selling potatoes, cheese and the

other products of the farm. My hon. friends opposite want to take away the pro. tection that the farmers have, the 20 per cent on potatoes, and allow the potatoes of their friends in Maine to come in and undersell our potatoes. Why did they not take that ground when the Laurier Administration increased the tariff on potatoes? Since 1896 the hon. member for Kings (Mr. Hughes) says that conditions have changed. Where is the change in conditions since the tariff on potatoes was increased from 15 cents to 20 cents? There is no ehange so far as I can see, and I venture to say there is not an hon. gentleman on the other side of the House who can show that there is any change in conditions to-day.

Might I ask the hon. gentleman a question? He wants to know what the change is, and why this resolution should not have been made prior to the present date? A very good answer is that the United States Government until last October had a duty ,of 25 cents a bushel against Canadian potatoes. Now they make the duty 10 per cent on condition that if we allow their potatoes in free, then, ipso facto, our potatoes go into the United States free.

And the hon. member for Kings, P.iE.I., and the hon. member for Carleton boast that the state of Maine, the state adjoining the province of New Eruns-wick, raised last year 18,000,000 bushels of potatoes; and you want the farmers of the state of Maine to come in and undersell our farmers. There is no doubt that is what you want. What change has taken place in the conditions? The only change is that we have a better market to-day than we had when the duty on potatoes was raised from 15 cents to 20 cents, by reason of the great industries that have been established and the increasing population which has come into the industrial centres, composed not of men engaged in agriculture, but of men engaged in manufacturing.
I wished particularly to make reference to the statement made by the hon. member for Kings that nothing was being done by the Department of Agriculture with reference to this matter. You see, Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman is now in Opposition and does not know what i3 going on. It is just as well that he should be made acquainted with the facts.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
The House has probably
learned more about potatoes .last evening and to-day than ever before in the history of Parliament, and I should be loth to burden the patience of the House by discussing at much greater length questions relating to that useful vegetable. There are one or two things however to which I wish to refer briefly and also to make a statement as to the position of the department on some matters that have been touched upon. In the first place, I can hardly see how in any case, a member on this side of the Hcuse understanding the nature of resolutions and what they mean can possibly vote lor so extraordinary a resolution as that moved by the hon. member for Northumberland, as follows:
That resolution 3, schedule * A,' be amended by adding after 79a, the following:
That tariff item No. 83 be amended by adding thereto the following words : Provided, however, that potatoes dry, desiccated or otherwise prepared, being the growth and production of the United States and shall be admitted free of duty when, and as soon as, the United States removes the embargo regulations now existing against like articles, the growth and production of Canada.
I do not know what unhappy confusion of thought exists in the hon. gentleman's nund that may have induced him to frame his resolution in these words. It means, if it means anything that the United States are absolutely insincere in putting on that embargo. It is perfectly true-and this rather conflicts with the statement of the hon. member for Carleton-that it has been urged, and urged not without some reason, that powerful commercial interests were at work in inducing the United States to put that embargo on. I am not making the statement, but I say it has been urged, and urged with some force. But my hon. friend who is so courteous to the United States and complains that we on this side are trying to establish unfriendly instead of friendly relations is dealing them the most unkindest cut of all when he says that they put on the embargo for reasons of this kind. If his resolution does not mean that it means nothing, for it in effect declares that we should have a reduction of duty against the United States in return for the wiping out of the restriction against disease. I should find it, therefore, impossible, whatever my opinion on the duty question, to vote for a resolution so un-

309i
sound. Speaking as a member 10 p.m. of this side and a member of the Government, I would certainly not vote for a resolution that would have the effect of wiping out the duty on an article produced so widely in our own country. I am not going to labour that point. In passing I might point out that my hon. friends opposite, especially those from the West, have a favourite way of stating the effect of duties on our products sent to the United States by saying that they pay the duty, but when an article is imported from the United States, they assume that they pay that duty also; but you cannot have it both going and coming. But, assume for the sake of the argument that the producer pays the duty on the potatoes exported from Canada to the United States, yet that duty is only ten per cent, and the price, if I remember the figures given by the hon. member for Carleton only forty cents per bushel, so that it would only amount to four cents per bushel. In order to wipe out a duty of four cents per bushel on our potatoes going to the United States, which it is not clear that the Canadian producer pays, the hon. gentleman is willing to abolish the twenty cents per bushel on potatoes coming into Canada which would be a hardship-

Forty cents peT bushel
is the average price under present conditions and has been for years past. But if the American market were free to us, it would be greater than that, and so it would mean the saving of I should think, five cents per bushel.
Mr. BURRELL; The difference is only one cent, and I will not dispute about that. But I am bound to say, with my limited knowledge-or perhaps a little more than limited knowledge-of the farming community of Canada as a whole, though perhaps New Brunswick is in a peculiar posi-* tion with regard to the United States market, the farmers of Canada, and especially those of my own province, would oppose and strongly condemn me if I advocated the removal of the duty of 20 per cent per bushel on potatoes. I do not wish to go into the question of duty, but merely wish to say that I would vote against the resolution for this reason as well as for the other that I pointed out.
Now, I desire to say a few words in regard to another feature of the discussion which occupied a good deal of time, namely, the question of the embargo and the po'tato disease, which led up to the embargo. As members of the House know,
the disease in question is a fungous disease, propagating once a year by spores, as all fungus growths do. We have lately heard much about two serious diseases. One of these diseases is potato canker or black canker of the potato. In 1910, the late Government issued an order prohibiting entirely the importation of potatoes from Newfoundland and from St. Pierre-Miquelon, for reasons that in those countries they had this canker, which was considered of a dangerous kind. In September, 1912, we got information that canker was very prevalent in certain parts of Europe, and that they were having great difficulty, especially in Great Britain, where they were quarantining large areas. After careful consideration, this Government issued an Order in Council prohibiting the importation of potatoes from Great Britain and from nearly all countries in Europe. This was followed shortly afterwards by action on the part of the United States of a similar kind, placing an absolute embargo on European countries for potato canker, which was admittedly a very serious disease. After we had done that, we thought it wise, as there had been some importations into Canada very few; not nearly so great importations as had been made into the United States before the embargo was put on;
I think there was a lot of 300,000 bushels arriving in Boston from Europe to bring to the attention of the the farmers in this country, and so we issued a circular from our department and a coloured poster along the line of, and a little smaller than, the one shown here today. This led to potatoes supposedly affected with canker, or some other disease, being sent from all parts of the country to our Dominion botanist. We detected the existence of powdery scab in various parts of the country, perhaps most heavily in Kamouraska, Quebec. Perhaps I should not name these places, as it does not help to have the places talked about, but, on the other hand, it is often well to give these matters publicity with a view to remedy, so on the whole it is probably better to state all the circumstances. This disease, powdery scab, was found very slightly in Nova Scotia; a good many cases-about fifteen I think at that time-in New Brunswick; and in Prince Edward Island, in a considerably greater number. I was rather astonished to hear the hon. member for Kings, Prince Edward Island (Mr. Hughes) -and he will correct me if I am wrong-

make in this House the extraordinary statement, the making of which, I think, shows that he is not familiar with farming problems and is not following attentively the progress ' of farming in Prince Edward Island-that no powdery scab existed in Prince Edward Island, nor any other disease. He stated that the American Consul, who, I suppose, is not considered a great authority on plant pathology, had made the statement that there was no powdery scab. And the hon. gentleman was surprised that the Government-I presumed he referred to the Prince Edward Island Government- did not at once confirm this statement.

I read from a paper published in Charlottetown, a statement to the effect that the American Consul had reported to his Government that there was no disease in the Prince Edward Island potatoes against which the United States were providing an embargo,-that the diseases were simply dry rot and wet rot. I did not vouch for that statement, I read the statement in a paper published in Charlottetown that the American Consul had made that report to his Government; I did not vouch for its authenticity at all. '

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I may have been wrong in assuming that my hon. friend endorsed that position, but I thought my hon. friend's argument led to the view that Prince Edward Island was free from this disease. I am surprised that the statement was made, and still more surprised that the hon. gentleman did not verify it before he cast blame upon the provincial Government for not backing up the statement of the American Consul, who evidently was not fully conversant with the subject. My hon. friend would only have to look up the annual report of the Dominion botanist to find where the disease existed and where it did not. While it is true that the distribution of the disease is rather widespread in Prince Edward Island, the infestation itself is comparatively slight. After we found out these things, we obtained the services of expert men-qualified plant pathologists who pay special attention to potato diseases-and sent them to Prince Edward Island and other points to examine carefully into the conditions so that we could take steps to educate the people to look after these things and to report if the existence of any of these diseases was discovered. I have given to this matter a great deal of attention, and I have never yet been convinced and never have seen reason to convince me that the powdery fMr. Burrell.]
scab is of as malignant a character as the potato canker, which probably justified the embargo against Europe and other countries where it existed. The spores of the canker remain dormant under ground for eight years, always ready, when potatoes are planted, to take active life and propagate the disease. While a similar state of things may exist in a smaller degree with regard to powdery scab, the methods of combating it are attended with greater success, and I am bound to say that I cannot regard powdery scab as being in the same category as the potato canker. In the fall of 1913 reports appeared in the press to the effect that the United States was contemplating taking action against Canada in the way of prohibiting the entry of her potatoes.
I would like to refer for a moment to the remarks of the hon. member for Carleton.
I shall not criticise what be said; I appreciate the kindly references he made to myself and to the efforts of the department in this regard, but I do gather that he thought that the Minister of Agriculture or the department was slow in taking the initial steps and that a much better arrangement cbuld have beep made at Washington if we had moved more quickly at the beginning. I know that my hon. friend does not want to be unfair, and I want to put him right on that matter. I received a wire from the hon. gentleman on November 26, and I think he will recall the fact that I wired him the following day assuring him that this matter had been under the consideration of the department and that we were giving it every possible attention. His letter arrived during the week; on account of the reports which were appearing in the press, I had quite a number of letters and telegrams from New Brunswick and elsewhere along the same line. Prior to that time we had unofficial knowledge of the matter through correspondence between the experts of our department and the experts of the United States department, and in the weekly news letter of the United States Department of Agriculture we had previously seen a paragraph, which was, in a sense, official, intimating that the question whether the United iStates should take action against Canada in the way of embargo was to be discussed. I had a memorandum prepared with regard to the matter before it was brought to my attention by our various friends and by the hon. member for Carle-

ton. We gave the matter further consideration. and within a day or two of that time we took it up through the ambassador at Washington. I ought to point out that we were not neglectful of the interests of Canada, or of New Brunswick potato shippers, because we knew very well that under the terms of the Federal Quarantine Act the United States could not take action of that kind without giving us an opportunity to be heard; consequently we did not feel any particular alarm that they would immediately	put on an embargo without
giving	us an	opportunity for consultation. But, to make assurance doubly sure, we took the matter up with the ambassador at Washington. We pointed out that we did not consider that this disease was sufficiently serious to warrant the action which had been reported by the press as 'ikely to be taken by the United States, and that if such action were seriously contemplated by the United States we trusted that they -would give us ample opportunity to prepare a case and to appear before them, either through the embassy at Washington or personally, to make arrangements with regard to the whole matter. This was done. As my hon. friend knows, we went to Washington; a conference was held on December 18 and the whole matter was gone into very thoroughly.
The hon. member for Carleton said something about Mr. Gussow, the Dominion botanist and plant pathologist. I understood him to say that while he did not criticise Mr. Gussow's technical qualifications, he did not think that he was. very practical. I may say in passing that Mr. Gussow's knowledge of plant diseases is looked upon with a great deal of respect by leading experts in the United States. In matters of this kind, therefore, we shall have to rest assured that Canada is being well represented so far as her export knowledge goes.
When was Mr. Gussow appointed?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
He was appointed by my predecessor and is, I believe, a well qualified official. We are giving him every opportunity to carry on his work in a larger and more extended way in the future. At that conference business interests were represented; there were present congressmen and representatives from various states interested in potato growing. A large number of petitions were received from persons representing the interests of what we
may call the commercial side of the potato industry. Although they would admit nothing in the way of infestation in their own country except an isolated case or two, it was pointed out at that conference by Mr. Gussow that we had knowledge of the fact that powdery scab did exist in Maine, Massachussets, Nebraska and Winconsin. I am not saying anything unfriendly, but it is not unfair to say that the proceedings at the conference were somewhat pro forma, and it was evident from what took place that the officials of the United States Department of Agriculture had made up their minds that an embargo of this kind would be placed upon Canadian potatoes. On December 22 they issued an order which took effect December 24, practically putting an embargo on our potatoes. Theoretically it was not, perhaps, an absolute embargo, inasmuch as they provided for the admission of our potatoes under certain restrictions.	.
But that is only another way of making an embargo, because the restrictions were such that it was impossible, in a practical commercial way, to ship potatoes into the country. Two of the conditions imposed were that there should be adequate field inspection, and also an adequate, clearly-defined location of infested areas. Hon. gentlemen who know anything about this matter can easily see that in December, when the crop was all harvested, some of it in the cellar and some in the hands of wholesalers, it would be quite impossible to make an adequate field inspection that year or to make a definition of infested areas that could possibly satisfy the United States authorities. That is why we regarded that as an embargo.

From any information which the minister may have from Washington, can he say if adequate inspection would mean inspection by. United States officers or would they accept the inspection of Canadian officers?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
They would require that inspection by our federal officers, Canadian officers, and it would have been impossible to carry that out. We have had many representations from New Brunswick and elsewhere, and some correspondence inviting us strongly to retaliate and put an embargo against the United States; others suggesting that we define the area. The more we looked into it the more difficult it seemed to deal with this particular condition of affairs. I did not think that

because we believed another nation had made a mistake in putting on such severe restrictions, we would have been justified in adopting similar action, and so we did not retaliate. Early this year the United States authorities had to admit, because the evidence was multiplied, that there was a very widespread infestation in the state of Maine. I must point out that until then they had made no restriction in the United States; although they must have known, and we pointed out to them, that they had the disease in various portions of that country. United States officers have practically admitted that they had made nothing like the investigations into this matter that we had made, and I wish to add as a compliment to our own Dominion botanist that the poster got out a year and a half ago in reference to potato canker has been used and copied, and our other publications have been copied and published in the United States, and they have formed no unimportant part in the United States work against potato diseases. I think that is a good tribute to Canadian energy in facing these things. As I said, the United States until lately had imposed no restrictions, but they put a restriction against the state of Maine. Then there came this question: they restricted the state of Maine to this extent that they prohibited Maine shippers sending potatoes into other portions of the United States except they had a certificate of freedom from disease from officers in Maine; but the restrictions imposed upon the state of Maine were nothing like so onerous and severe as those imposed against 'Canada in the regulations published in order No. IX of December 18. So we again, quite recently, have taken the matter up with the Embassy at Washington, and the Embassy, at our request, have made strong representations to the Department of Agriculture at Washington that they should give us just the same treatment in Canada that they are giving to Maine in regard to shipments into other states. We have not had any answer to that. I am not aware whether they will do it. I am not now criticising them except that I do say that they should, logically and fairly, give us as fair treatment in Canada as they gave their own state when they quarantined it for the same disease. While this matter was under discussion an international conference to deal with the whole question of plant diseases was called to meet in Rome.

Mr. Gussow represented Canada. The United States was invited to be present, and it was understood that the head of their board for dealing with these diseases would attend; but unfortunately and unhappily the United States was not represented at that conference at all. The French Government proposed a resolution that all vegetation and grain should be required to carry certificates of freedom from disease before being allowed to go from nation to nation. jThis, however, was woted down. The question of the preparation of a definite list of quarantinable diseases was discussed. So far as the powdery scab was concerned, each nation was left to deal with it as it wished. We have fairly good evidence in the department that powdery scab has been in Canada for six or seven years, and possibly before that. I think we are justified in assuming it has been in the United States a great deal longer than that. We have got it from them, or they from us, or we may both have got it from Europe. We undoubtedly have not hitherto considered the powdery scab as the same malignant and sinister character as potato canker. I am not minimizing the fact that it is a serious disease and that farmers should use every method to stamp it out, and I am also strongly of the opinion that the federal and provincial Governments should do everything that can be done to aid the farmer and to bring about a wholesale cooperation between the people and the Governments resulting in stamping out powdery scab. As far as this Government is concerned, we are going to give every possible assistance.
The question of the regulations of the embargo must necessarily be left now for a time until we begin to deal with another crop. I notice the United States are putting on a further quarantine which does not take place until next August, so we will. in the meantime have opportunity to consider the whole matter. In the meantime, this year we can only do our best by carrying on a campaign of education. We have added a number of men to our staff for temporary purposes. It is difficult to get good men, skilled in this work. We have engaged the services of Professor Adams, of the Science College of Dublin, who has made a specialty of potato diseases. He has entered the Canadian service, and will be put in charge of a lot of this work. We intend to try to educate the people to plant nothing but clean seed, to use fresh ground

and to take every step possible to help us stamp out the disease, and I think it can be stamped out.
Something has been said about the publication distributed to the members of this House. I am not saying this in any spirit of boasting, as the entire publication has been prepared in the department, but I believe that publication is a credit to the Dominion of Canada. I do not believe that there has been another publication of the kind on the continent as good and as thoroughly reliable and lifelike in regard to illustration or more helpful in respect to methods of eradication of the disease.
That pamphlet cost the department about $3,000. I think it is money well spent. If it is necessary to spend more I think it will be well spent. We have now 165,000 copies of it, 125,000 in English and 40,000 in French, which we intend to have widely distributed. I venture to say that our friends in the United States will take particular interest in it and will try and copy our action in that respect.
I can only express my apologies for taking up so much of the time of the committee. The country may rest assured that in so far as this matter is concerned, the Department of Agriculture and the Government will take every step that can be taken in co-operation with everybody concerned to stamp out the disease.
Would the minister indicate the steps that can be taken by the farmers in planting their seed in order to take precautions against the disease? Can the seed Ibe soaked?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
No, that matter is all
covered by the directions in the pamphlet. With regard to several of these diseases, including this one, you can do nothing in the way of soaking seed or treatment of any kind. The only method of value is to plant clean seed. You must not only not take seed from a crop that may seem to be sound, but you must take seed from a crop that has never had the disease and plant it in soil where diseased crops have never been grown. My hon. friend will find that the pamphlet is very full and explicit. The information is packed into small compass, but it will give immense help to potato growers, and in addition the services of our officers will be at the disposal of anybody in the country who wants to make use of them.

I was very much
pleased to hear the remarks of the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Burrell), and especially was I pleased when he spoke of the efforts that the Government were making to induce the Government of the United States to place no more stringent regulations upon the importation of potatoes from Canada than they were putting on potatoes from the state of Maine. That was especially gratifying to me, because it shows clearly that, in the opinion of the minister and the Government, they value highly the market of the United States for Canadian potatoes.
Oh, oh.

No better argument
could be used. Why, if they did not value that market, were such efforts put forth to get the regulations against this country made no stricter than against the state of Maine? No better argument could be used in favour of the value of that market and no stronger one could be advanced in favour of the reduction of the duty on potatoes into this country in order to obtain free access to the American market.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We are in committee and I avail myself of the privilege of speaking twice. I am the more inclined to this course because otherwise I might appear to be somewhat discourteous to my hon. friend from Northumberland (Mr. Loggie). I am sure he will acquit me of any intention of that character. When I expressed the desire between twelve and one o'clock last night that the debate should be concluded, if possible, before the House rose, I had no idea that so many gentlemen intended to take part in this discussion, and that it would range over so large a field. Otherwise, of course, I should have been more than willing that the House should have adjourned and that the debate should have been continued to-day. The hon. member for Northumberland has offered an amendment, and in order that we may see precisely what we are debating, I propose to read the resolution which is offered for the consideration of the committee:
That tariff item No. 83 be amended by adding thereto the following words:	Provided,
however, that potatoes dry, desiccated or otherwise prepared, being the growth and production of the United States, shall be admitted free of duty when, and as soon as, the United States removes the embargo regulations now

existing against like articles, the growth and production of Canada.
My hon. friend is evidently of the view that if this resolution were adopted and the tariff change which he has in mind made, the potatoes mentioned in the tariff item would be .admitted free from the United States only, and that by reason of their free admission into this country Canada would become entitled to the benefits of the countervailing provisions of the Underwood tariff and that our potatoes would be given free access to the markets of the United States. I think that is a fair deduction from the wording of the resolution. I would point out to my hon. friend certain consequences that would flow if this tariff change were made. In the first place, we would have to admit free potatoes from the United States and from all the Britsh colonies and British possessions.
I understood that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend says that he understood that. I notice that he did not emphasize it. My hon. friend knows also that there are certain nations which are accorded most favoured nation treatment under the tariff laws of Canada.
That is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Among these are the Argentine republic, Austria-Hungary, Denmark, Japan, Norway, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland and Venezuela. In passing, I must express my surprise that such a good free trader as we have always understood the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) to be, should take exception to potatoes coming into Canada from Germany. I understood my hon. friend to be reluctant to admit that he should like to see potatoes coming into Canada from Germany.

My hon. friend understood me absolutely correctly. I do not want to see them coming from Germany, because I do not think Germany has ever given us fair treatment and because German potatoes are diseased.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend says the reason is because they are diseased.
This would not bring them from Germany.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Is it a fact that my hon. friend is objecting that cheaper potatoes would come into Canada from Germany, or some other nation, and break the price in Canada ?
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend puts it entirely on the ground of disease.
I would like to ask the minister if Germany admits our potatoes free.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am unable, offhand, to answer that question.
I can tell you: They do not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Surely a good free trader who is in favour of free food could not by any possibility object to Canada buying cheaper potatoes, whether they come from
Germany or any other country.
Purely for information, may I ask the minister if an effort was not made some years ago to have the most favoured nation clauses cancelled ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am coming to that in a moment. No less a personage than the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) moved a resolution in the Imperial conference having as its object the denunciation of those treaties.
And that was passed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Passed by the Imperial Conference.
And they agreed to. cancel them whenever Canada wanted them cancelled.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend from Carle-ton was evidently of the view, or he gave the committee the view, that the United States Congress had made these countervailing provisions in respect to potatoes having in mind especially Canada
I thought so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend surely does not argue that the provisions of the Underwood tariff are limited to Canada? I have those provisions here, and I will read them to my hon. friend. I quote from the free list of the Underwood tariff:
Potatoes, and potatoes dried, desiccated, or otherwise prepared, not specially provided for in this section: Provided, that any of the foregoing specified articles shall he subject to a duty of ten per cent ad valorem when imported directly or indirectly from a country, dependency, or other subdivision of government, which imposes a duty on such articles imported from the United States.
Therefore the legislation is general to those countries which will admit potatoes the product of the United States free. The United States will extend the same privi-

lege to them. That is the effect of this provision of the Underwood tariff.
I listened with as much interest and attention as to anything in the House, to the recital of my hon. friend (Mr. Carvell) as to what was done by the Maine farmers as soon as the Underwood tariff reduced the duty upon potatoes to ten per cent, ad valorem. I may say that under the Canadian tariff the duty upon potatoes is twenty cents a bushel, and that previously to the introduction of the Underwood tariff the duty upon potatoes in the United States was twenty-five cents a bushel. By the Underwood tariff the duty upon potatoes was reduced to ten per cent ad valorem, which is the rate to-day. The recital of my hon. friend (Mr. Carvell) wTas most graphic and illuminating, and I could . not help but reflect upon the strange irony of political circumstances. I have not the slightest doubt-and I am not going to hark back to the reciprocity agreement-that my hon. friend went upon the platforms of New Brunswick and, powerful debater as he is, set forth to the people the advantages of the reciprocity agreement, under which Canadian potatoes would be admitted free to the markets of the United States. Mark you, at that time the duty on potatoes entering the United States from Canada was twenty-five cents a bushel, and my hon. friend naturally concluded that if that duty of twenty-five cents a bushel were removed, the potatoes of his native province would gain free access to the markets of the United States. Let us see what happened.
Following on the enactment of the Underwood tariff which did not abolish the duty but reduced it to ten per cent ad valorem, the Maine farmers, who appear to value protection pretty highly, at once sent agents, as I understood my hon. friend to say, through the province of New Brunswick, to ascertain if there was any disease in potatoes which they could 'bring to the notice of the Government at Washington. He also told us that New Brunswick was capable of multiplying threefold, yes tenfold, her present production of potatoes. Is there any doubt whatever that the Maine farmers had that capacity of potato production in New Brunswick in view when they initiated the proceedings which led to this embargo. I put it to my hon. friend (Mr. Carvell) does he believe that if the United States duty upon potatoes had remained at twenty-five cents per bushel, that embargo would be in existence to-day?
I do not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend does not believe, and I do not believe it would be in existence to-day, if the duty of twenty-five cents a bushel had remained. The result then is that the reduction by the Underwood tariff from twenty-five cents a bushel to ten per cent ad valorem has caused the potato growers of New Brunswick to be absolutely shut out of the markets of the United States. Now, if that happened on a reduction to ten per cent ad valorem would it not have happened or something worse, if possible, if the duty had been entirely removed? I cannot help but reflect upon the strange irony of circumstances, which sent my hon. friend on the platforms of New Brunswick to point out the advantages which would be gained by the farmers of New Brunswick by reason of the reciprocity agreement which would admit their potatoes free to' the American markets, thus enabling them to double, and treble, and multiply by ten, their output, and today forces him in this House to point out, that because of the reduction by the Underwood Tariff to ten per cent ad valorem, on the initiative the farmers of the United States who he said had strong political influence, the New Brunswick farmers are shut out *absolutely from the markets of the United States, and they are not in as good a position as they were before.
I said on the initiative of the farmers of the state of Maine not of the United States as a whole.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Maine is a powerful and
influential state. The Minister of Agriculture said that at the conference which was held with respect to this question, commercial interests were represented as well. I desire to make no strong statements about this matter, because I was not before aware of the facts which have been called to the attention of the House this afternoon by my hon. friend from Carleton and by the Minister of Agriculture. But, is there any doubt that the farmers of Maine themselves, and through their political representatives, brought powerful influence to bear upon the Government of the United States, and that as a result this embargo was established? There is no doubt about it whatever. Therefore, I say that the farmers cf New Brunswick are in a worse position than they would have been if the tariff of twenty-five cents a bushel had remained against Canadian potatoes, because the Canadian farmers would have at least been

able to sell in the markets of the United States after the payment of the twenty-five cents per 'bushel duty. I point out to my hon. friend from Northumberland (Mr. Loggie) that the hon. gentleman from Carleton (Mr. Carvetl), in my judgment has this afternoon supplied the strongest possible argument against the adoption of his resolution. If the amendment of my hon. friend (Mr. Loggie) were adopted, what would follow? If the United States removes the embargo, then by reason of the countervailing provisions of the Underwood tariff, the potatoes of Canada would gain free entry to the markets of the United States. I put it to my hon. friend from Northumberland that if the farmers of Maine have taken the initiative and have by the influence they have been able to bear had this embargo put on because of a reduction of twenty-five cents a bushel to ten per cent ad valorem, what would they not do if this amendment were carried and they knew that the potatoes from Canada would go into the United States, not at <& duty of ten per oent ad valorem but absolutely free of duty? That argument cannot be refuted. If the farmers of Maine had taken the initiative, and my hon. friend criticised them pretty roughly for doing so, to get an embargo placed on our potatoes because of a reduction in the duty, what would they not be disposed to do if the duty were wiped off altogether and they found themselves exposed to Canadian competition?
I need not tell my hon. friend from Carleton, who has a strong, virile intellect, what would happen under such circumstances. He knows that if this amendment were to pass this House the efforts of the Maine farmers would be redoubled.

Does my hon. friend
want me to tell him what I know?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Very well.

I know no such thing,
and I tell him frankly that I do not believe the competition from the province of New Brunswick would affect the price of potatoes one cent in the United States, nor do I believe that the United States people would have attempted to put on this embargo so far as Canada is concerned. It was the European market they were afraid of. The hon. gentleman is harking back to reciprocity, but I can tell him that all of this trouble dates from the refusal of reei-
[Mr. W. T. White 1
procity, and had reciprocity gone through there would have been' an embargo against the rest of the world and there would not be an embargo against Canada to-day.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
We do not produce
enough.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I assume that the Maine farmers, to whom my hon. friend has paid a high tribute this afternoon, are a keenwitted, practical-minded set of men.
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Will my hon. friend tell me why they took the trouble to send over agents to New Brunswick to see if they could find an example of powdery scab, in order that potatoes of New Brunswick might be debarred from the American market ?

With the greatest of
pleasure. I live alongside of those people; I know the men who have made the incursion into New Brunswick, and I have it from the potato men and the potato growers of the state of Maine. They did not fear the Canadian competition; but they were determined to prevent the free importation of potatoes into the United States from every country of the world, and they got their Government to put on this embargo in order to shut out the competition from Europe. When they shut out the competition from Europe, they wanted to shut it out from every country. Any one in the state of Maine will tell you that they did not fear the competition of New Brunswick or of Canada. If the competition only came from Canada, you would hear nothing about it; it was the competition from Europe that they desired to shut * out.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: My hon. friend's argument is a little faulty, inasmuch as the United States had already a very effective embargo against Europe on account of canker, which is a different thing entirely.

They had no embargo
against powdery scab, and it is professedly only against powdery scab that they are endeavouring to prohibit importations of potatoes from New Brunswick and other provinces of Canada into their country.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: My hon. friend did not understand me.

I did, and I think my hon. friend will see that I did before I have finished. They did not profess to put an embargo on potatoes on account of canker; they professed to do so on account of powdery scab. It is a fact that hundreds of thousands of bushels of European potatoes came into the United States from the 3rd day of October to the 24th day of December, 1913, from those countries which the United States believed did not possess canker, but did possess powdery scab. It was canker they were afraid of; and it was the fact that not merely a few carloads but whole shiploads of cankered potatoes came from Europe that made them determined to prohibit the importation of those potatoes, if possible.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I am afraid my hon.
friend has made rather a wild statement. I do not think he can show that thousands and thousands of bushels of potatoes came from European countries to the United States prior to their action, because they had an effective embargo against all countries on account of potato canker.

My hon. friend the
Minister of Agriculture is. all wrong.
Oh, oh.

I advise my hon. friends not to get too gay over it. My hon. friend, if he looks up the trade returns, will find that shipload after shipload of potatoes came from Europe into the ports of Boston and New York in November and early in December.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend
will have some difficulty in making the country believe that, if the Maine farmers had in view only the prohibition of the importation of potatoes from Europe, they would seek to accomplish their purpose by making an investigation of the farms in the province of New Brunswick. There is no doubt about it whatever, and my hon. friend has supplied the reason in his own argument. He says that New Brunswick is capable of increasing its output of potatoes tenfold. Does he mean to tell hon. members that, having regard to freight rates and all the other matters that enter into the question of price, an increase of the potato-product of New Brunswick by ten will have no material influence upon the price in the nearby markets of the United States?
Does my hon. friend not know that the freight rate to the United States is greater from New Brunswick than from Europe?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend says that they can keep out the European product by reason of canker.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend knows just as well as I do that, if the Canadian output were increased by ten, and if the farmers had free access to the markets of the United States and sent in their products subject to a 10 per cent or other duty, it would have a material influence upon the price in the nearby markets of the United States.
I do not think so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend does not think so, but some of us do think so. The Maine farmers thought so, and their action was governed by what they thought. They came in and examined the farms of New Brunswick; they found powdery scab; they brought political influence to bear, and they had this embargo enforced against the potatoes of Canada. The farmers in my hon. friend's constituency are in worse case to-day, as I said, than they would have been under the Payne-Aldrich tariff of the United States, namely, 25 cents a bushel upon potatoes. That is the result of the reduction in the tariff of the United States, which I have no doubt my hon. friend has heralded as a great advantage to Canada.
There aTe a few other statements which my hon. friend made to which I wish to refer briefly. Before doing so, I wish to say that if the amendment of my hon. friend from Northumberland, N.B. (Mr. Loggie), were adopted, and the tariff reduced, the result, in my judgment, would be that the present embargo would be made perpetual against the potatoes of Canada, because I believe the farmers of Maine, realizing as they would that this would mean, in the event of the removal of the embargo, the free 'entry of Canadian potatoes into the United States in competition with theirs, would exert their influence more strongly even than they did on the last occasion. The result would be that the Canadian potatoes would be absolutely shut out under an, embargo provision for all time from the markets of the United States.
My hon. friend said in the course of his remarks that the Canadian market would be of no advantage to the producers in the United States. That would seem to follow from his argument that prices were higher

in the United States than in Canada. If that is so, I would put it to my hon. friend, what possible influence upon the action of the United States could we exercise by the removal of our duty against potatoes? If the market of Canada is of no value to the potato growers of the United States, I repeat, what influence would any action on our part in removing or reducing the duty on potatoes have upon the Government of the United States with respect to the embargo? My hon. friend confutes lids own argument by his admission. Further, I put this to my hon. friend. He stated this afternoon that the United States acted fairly in imposing the embargo. What follows firom his argument? He said in substance and effect: If you will remove the duty, we may look for an earlier removal of the embargo. What has he suggested in that? That the embargo might be continued beyond the time during which it is properly enforcible; in other words, that it might become a protection to the farmers of the United States instead of a quarantine measure.
That absolutely follows from the argument of my hon. friend; there is no getting away from it. The Minister of Agriculture said, referring to the resolution of the hon. member for Northumberland, that there is confusion of thought in that resolution. My hon. friend from Carleton has argued this afternoon that the market of Canada is of no use to the potato growers of the United States. He has argued, notwithstanding that admission, that it will be influential in having the embargo removed so far as Canada is concerned if we remove the Canadian duty and admit American potatoes to this market, which according to his own statement, would he of no advantage to the United States. And he has 'by implication charged the United States with imposing this embargo, not for quarantine reasons, not for the purpose of keeping out disease, but solely as a protective measuie for their own farmers suffering from a reduction of the rates of duty under the provisions of the Underwood Tariff.
Let me put it another way:
11 p.m. The hon. gentleman knows that there are only two classes in the community who would be affected by an alteration in the tariff Tates-the consumers and the producers. If there is no advantage to the producer of potatoes in the United States in having access to the Canadian market, is there any advantage to the consumer in the United States in having the American tariff reduced or removed? If my

hon. friend says there is, I say the remedy is wholly in the hands of the United States: they can lower or remove their duty whenever they please.
Now, my hon. friend has spoken rather contemptuously of the home market.
Quite so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: His words were: The home market and all that sort of nonsense.
I meant all that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am sorry the hon. gentleman meant it, because I think he is a man capable of taking a broader view.
I have had experience.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Probably in one section of the country only. But we must learn that in this country there are many children of Confederation, there are many provinces, and what is an immortal truth in Nova Scotia may be a heresy in British Columbia. That is brought home to me every day in connection with such matters as the tariff. I am the first to admit that there are sections of Canada in which there is a considerable advantage in having access to the American market; I have always admitted that. But the hon. gentleman must take -the country as a whole. If he would visit to the province of Ontario or to the province of Quebec or many other provinces, he would find that the home market is not regarded as a bit of 'nonsense' by the agriculturists. I doubt if my hon. friend could carry his* membership in any rural constituency in Ontario if he came out and talked about the ' nonsense ' of the home market. I would point out that it was the appreciation by the Ontario farmer and the Quebec farmer of his home market that won the election on the reciprocity issue.
And I want to say that the election was won on money and the Ne Temere decree.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not propose to bandy words with my hon. friend on any proposition so foolish as that. I have stumped Ontario, and know rural Ontario as well; I was born on an Ontario farm, and I know farming conditions. It is true not only of Ontario but of Quebec, and of British Columbia and of Manitoba, and I believe it will be increasingly true of other provinces, that the farmer values greatly his home market. And my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), who committed himself for the

moment to a free food policy at Hamilton, had to back up on that policy because of the condition that I have mentioned as existing-namely, the appreciation by the Canadian farmer of feis home market.
How is he going to lose it in the event of reciprocity?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend knows the difference between a home market and a foreign market.

Do I understand the
hon. minister to assert that in the event of reciprocity in potatoes between Canada and the United States our farmers would lose the home market? Surely he does not undertake to assert such a proposition.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Let me say this to my hon. friend. Take the case of manufactures-

Just one moment. I understood the hon. member for Carleton to say that there was considerable nonsense in hon. gentlemen opposite continually asserting the great importance of the home market when any one on this side suggests the desirability of having a market for their products where there is an exportable surplus.
I was talking about the home market for potatoes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Carleton does not need an interpreter; whatever faults he may have, vagueness is not one of them. I understand him, and he knew I understood him. He cast contempt upon the home market.
For potatoes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
For potatoes and other
produce. He is a free trader for every part of Canada except New Brunswick, and a free trader there in everything except potatoes. He reminds me of the lines in the Biglow paper:
I du believe in Freedom's cause,
Ez fur away ez Payris is;
I love to see her stick her claws In them infernal Phayrisees.
So, with the hon. gentleman, protection is anathema on everything except the potatoes of New Brunswick. Now, I wish to say to him-because I have a good deal of respect for his ability and would like to see him take a larger view of this matter-that he cannot formulate a tariff policy by keeping in view only one province or one constituency; he must consider Canada as a whole. He is disregarding an obvious and patent
fact if he jumps to the conclusion that the farmer of this country does not value his home market. If he does not want to take my word for it, let him have a heart to heart talk with his right hon. leader (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) who had to withdraw from the policy set forth so eloquently in Hamilton because the rural members in Ontario and Quebec said to him: You aire going to ruin us in our constituencies. That is what I meant when I said that free food means free trade. And it does; because if the protective duties that have been valued by the farmers since protection was introduced in 1879 are to be swept away, they will insist that others be swept away also; they all stand on the same footing, and when the farmer of Ontario and of other provinces values his protection so much, he is either going to have it or see that nobody else shall have it.

Did I understand the minister to say that even if it could be shown that with potatoes on the free list in Canada and the United States it would be utterly impossible for the United States to send into this country potatoes in any substantial quantities and yet we could export in large quantitie? to the United States, he would still oppose the principle of this resolution?
In Canada-and that he would adhere to a tariff upon potatoes simply because the placing of potatoes upon the free list would disturb the whole fabric of protection. Does my hon. friend mean that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am of the opinion that
Canada should make her own tariffs, and that the United States and every other country should make their own tariffs. I believe in having a policy to work upon; I do not believe in taking isolated articles here and there, and for political, demagogic or other reasons, singling them out for special tariff treatment.

We are talking about
potatoes in this resolution.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I know that, but my hon. friend asked me for a general statement of opinion and I say that a minister of Finance should have a policy to work to. I 'aid down in my Budget speech a policy of reasonable protection for the industries of Canada, including agriculture, and I say, therefore, that you must deal with the products of agriculture as you deal with the



products of manufacture; that is to say you must afford them reasonable protection. How much that reasonable protection should be at any given time I do not propose to say, because as conditions change from time to time, necessary tariff modifications have to be made. There might come a time when certain manufactured, articles on which hitherto a duty has been imposed might be placed upon the free list; there might come a time when certain articles the product of the farm might well be placed upon the free list. But I lay down the general principle that the fiscal policy of the Government, as stated in the Budget speech, is one of reasonable protection for all the industries of Canada, including the great basic industry of agriculture. In the application of that principle we must be guided by the facts and conditions that are before us from time to time. I think that the resolution of the hon. member for Northumberland should be negatived, on several grounds. In the first place, it could not-and he evidently had in mind that it could-be confined to potatoes coming in from the United States of America. If the resolution were adopted, potatoes would come in from the United Kingdom, from all the British possessions and from all the most favoured nations. When my hon. friend (Mr. Car-veil) this afternoon indicated that he would be, to say the least, reluctant tfyat potatoes should come into Canada from Germany or from any other nation but the United States free of duty, I could not help thinking of what his leader did at the Imperial Conference in 1911. This is the resolution which was moved by my right hon. friend and adopted by the Imperial Conference at that time:
That His Majesty's Government be requested to open negotiations with the several foreign governments having treaties which apply to the overseas Dominions with a view to securing liberty for any of those Dominions which may so desire to withdraw from the operation of the treaty without impairing the treaty in respect of the rest of the empire.
My right hon. friend obviously had in mind at that time the idea that these treaties should be denounced in order that these commodities should not come in free by reason of the reciprocity pact. My hon. friend a few moments ago said that he objected to potatoes coming in from Germany free of duty only on account of their being affected with disease.
I did not say so; my hon. friend said that for me.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
What did my hon. friend
say ?
My hon. friend drew that inference from my remarks; I did not make the statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: On what ground is my hon. friend unwilling that potatoes should enter New Brunswick from Germany free of duty?
I will answer when my hon. friend is through.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I asked my hon. friend a few minutes ago whether he objected to pototoes coming into Canada from Germany free of duty on the ground that it would make them cheaper in New Brunswick, and I understood him to say-and by reason of what he said he got into a controversy with the Minister of Agriculture- that he objected on account of their being diseased. If this is the only reason, then does he subscribe to what was done by his leader at the Imperial Conference in 1911, whereby the right hon. gentleman desired to have the treaties denounced in order that these goods might enter Canada free of duty?
Absolutely.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If my hon. friend does not want to see natrural and manufactured products come from the most favoured nations free of duty, is he a free trader or is he a protectionist? If my hon. friend is not a protectionist, what objection has he to natural and manufactured products coming into Canada free of duty from the most favoured nations?
As I have said, the resolution of the hon. member for Northumberland should be negatived, on several grounds. One of them is that the goods from these other nations that I have mentioned would be admitted free to the markets of Canada. Secondly, as pointed out by the Minister of Agriculture, the resolution on the face of it implies that the United States has imposed this embargo for other than quarantine reasons. Th'ere is no getting away from that fact; the implication is evident from the arguments that followed. The implication of the hon. mem her for Northumberland and of the hou member for Carleton is that if Canada will place potatoes on the free list, the United States will be more likely, in the early future, to remove the embargo. On what ground should the United States remove the embargo? Only on the ground that,

from the standpoint of quarantine and the interests of agriculture, there is no longer any necessity for it. My hon. friend has admitted that the Canadian market is of no value to the American farmer; yet he says that the American Government will be prone to remove this embargo at an earlier date if we admit their potatoes into Canada free of duty.
The third reason why the resolution of my hon. friend should not be accepted is that, as I stated last night, it is inconsistent with the fiscal policy of protection that I laid down in the Budget speech. I do not say, and I never have said, that a policy of protection means that no articles produced or manufactured in Canada should be placed upon the free list. On the contrary, I have said in my Budget speech and on other occasions that as conditions change, tariff modifications may be made; that duties may be reduced or wholly abolished as circumstances may permit or as the public interest may require. But, having regard to the facts adduced this evening by the hon. member for Frontenac and others as to the production of potatoes in Canada and in the United States, I say that the time has not come when we should place potatoes upon the free list; that to do so under the existing circumstances would be inconsistent with the fiscal policy of protection which I enunciated in the Budget speech. For all these reasons, therefore, I ask that this amendment be negatived.

My hon. friend assumes that I announced in this House that I was an absolute free trader.
