I think he would have some difficulty in finding record of my having made any such assertion, either in this House or on the platforms of this country, wherever I have discussed these questions-and I have been discussing them for a great many years. I am not like my hon. friend, who is hidebound to some particular policy and cannot get away from it. I believe in a business tariff. If it is necessary to put on a reasonable amount of protection for business reasons, I am willing to have it put on. On the other hand, if good business dictates that a thing should be put on the free list, I am for putting it on tne free list. I do not think my hon. friend can make very much capital by charging me with being neither free trader nor protectionist. I try to look at this thing from the business standpoint.
My hon. friend also brought up the question of the favoured nations. I did not in-196i
tend to hark back to reciprocity and refrained from saying anything about what the result would have been if reciprocity had passed. I am one of those who said in 1911 that reciprocity was not dead and I say so now. It is as much alive to-day as ever and will always be until the matter is settled properly. The right hon. the leader of the Opposition, when he attended the Imperial Conference of 1911, secured the passage of a resolution favouring the abrogation of the favoured nation treaties so far as Canada is concerned. This was done for the purpose of putting Canada in a position to abrogate and get rid of these treaties if we wanted to do so. I do not want to allow Germany to send potatoes into Canada if we cannot get a corresponding advantage from them. The same thing applies to Denmark, Holland, Belgium or any other country. I do not know that I would be so patriotic that I would like Great Britain or anybody else to send potatoes in here if I did not think it would be to our benefit as well as to theirs. Therefore, when our friend harks back to the favoured nation treaties he knows that the resolution of my bon. friend from Northumberland has nothing to do with favoured nations, because under the resolution passed by the Imperial Conference, if this Government wants to they can denounce the treaty as against Germany or any other country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Is the hon. member in
favour of putting on the free list all live stock and other products of agriculture in Canada either from Germany or any other country?

There may be a few exceptions but as a general principle it would be absolutely so and I think it is in the best interests of both producer and consumer in Canada. I would not say that there might not 'be a few exceptions because no person should be called on without going over the list to give an absolute answer to such a question. As a general thing I believe it would be of great benefit to the people of Canada as a whole. Therefore, I think we can dismiss the result of the favoured nation treaties on this question of potatoes. I stated that the result of this treaty would be to allow the potatoes from Great Britain to come in here free and I have no fault to find with potatoes coming from Great Britain provided they are not prevented by quarantine regulations of some kind.
My hon. friend talked about the home market and tried to show that I was inconsistent in my statement about it being

of no value to the American producer. I stated that I did not believe the free entry of potatoes into Canada would be of any advantage to the American farmer. I said I believed that the American Government might have thought it to be of some advantage or they would not have insisted in their tariff that our potatoes would not enter their country without a corresponding concession on our part. My friends from Ontario, from whom all the opposition has come, do not seem to realize that they do not produce anything like the potatoes which they consume in Ontario.
You do not know what you are talking about.

The hon. gentleman does not and I know what I am talking about. If the hon. gentleman goes to the Canadian Pacific railway office in Montreal he will find that for the last five or' six years we have been exporting into Ontario from New Brunswick anywhere from 500,000 bushels to 1,000,000 bushels a yeajr. These are pretty big figures but' we cannot find them in the trade returns because there are no returns for interprovincial trade. The price of potatoes all over the cities of Ontario is entirely governed by the price of potatoes in New Brunswick. New Brunswick potatoes are quoted at from 5 to 10 cents a bag more than the native potatoes. When the American market was practically open to us in October, November and December of 1913 our potatoes practically all went to the American market. Dealers in New Brunswick told me that where they send one car to the Canadian market they send ten to the American. Therefore the price in Ontario of New Brunswick potatoes was governed entirely by the price in Boston and the price of New Brunswick potatoes coverns the price of the home product in Ontario. If you take away from Ontario the potatoes we have been sending you- and that will be the result of opening the American market-you will be creating a demand for Ontario potatoes that you have not to-day, you will be compelled to raise half a million bushels a year more.
We do not get a New Brunswick potato in the neighbourhood of Peterborough.
My hon. friend does not know. They get them anyway in Muskoka, which is farther away than Peterborough.
I know a potato dealer very well and he says that.

If my hon. friend will
go to his potato dealer and ask him if there has not been a carload of New Brunswick potatoes sold in Peterborough this year, I am satisfied that he will learn that they have been sold; and if he sends a telegram this minute I will pay for the telegram and the reply.

You need not. I will tell you something shorter and quicker than that. Senator Ferguson's son from Prince Edward Island is a particular friend of mine in Peterborough, and he deals in potatoes. When there is a shortage in Peterborough through drouth he gets his potatoes from Prince Edward Island; he does not get them at all from New Brunswick.

There was a time in the spring of 1912 when -some potatoes were sent from Prince Edward Island to Peterborough. I happen to have a big lawsuit in progress now over a shipment and I hope to fight it out before very long and of course I want to win; but my horn, friend is evidently not aware that they cannot get potatoes from Prince Edward Island from the last of December until the 1st of April because there is no practical way of getting them across the straits and they have to have them in Peterborough during the winter.
I am telling you facts. It is no use frying to put that down my throat.

I think it is a'helpless case; if my hon. friend will not believe me when I tell him that you cannot economically get them across the straits in winter time, I have nothing more to say to him. If he will consult his friends from Prince Edward Island I think he will find that I am pretty nearly correct. If ever theTe was a chance for my hon. friend to use an aeroplane in a commercial way it would be in getting potatoes across the straits in the winter time. However, the home market in Ontario would be immensely benefited by the reduction of this duty or the making of potatoes free in the United States because it would absolutely divert from Ontario the half million bushels which we are sending annually from the Maritime provinces.
Mr. DeWITT FOSTER: Will the price go up?

Will it go up to the
Ontario farmer?
Yes.
Of course it will.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: How will that affect the consumer?

After the very lucid explanation which the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Burrell) gave, and in which he stated that there was reason for the American Government putting an embargo on potatoes from the Maritime provinces, was it wise for the Minister of Finance to charge a great and friendly nation like the United States with sharp practice in putting on that embargo against Canada? I think nobody can take any other meet meaning out of the hon. gentleman's speech.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This was my argument, and it was perfectly plain: I said that some of the Maine farmers upon the reduction of the duties by the Underwood tariff, had sent agents to New Brunswick, according to the statement of the hon. member for Carieton (Mr. Carvell), to ascertain if there was any powdery scab upon the potatoes raised there. I said that they had taken the initiative, and I also said-and I think that my hon. friend agreed with me^-that if the duty had not been reduced the farmers would not have taken the initiative, and would not have brought the influences to bear which resulted in the investigation. I did not say then, and I do not say now, that the officials of the United States who held this investigation acted with any impropriety but that they would not have acted at all if the Maine farmers, of whom my hon. friend spoke this afternoon, had not taken the-initiative. I believe he agreed with that, view. I do not know if there is any powdery scab on the potatoes of New Brunswick or not, and I do not know whether the hon. Minister of Agriculture said there was or not. I was not dealing with the question of whether -there was or not. I was dealing with this only, that by reason of the reduction of the tariff the farmers of Maine had taken the initiative which had brought about the embargo. I do not say whether it was properly imposed; I do not know whether it was or not. But I say that the amendment of the hon. member for Northumberland, and the arguments which have been used in support of it, to the effect that the United States would be inclined to put an end to the embargo at an earlier date than they otherwise would if we gave free access for their potatoes to our markets, cast doubt upon their good faith in continuing the embargo. I did not cast that doubt. My hon. friend (Mr. Nesbitt) had better look to his own side for the implication, because I have made none. I have been dealing with the resolution, and I take the same view of it as was taken by my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture, namely, that its effect is to cast doubt upon the good faith of the United States Government in maintaining that embargo. I have made no such statement as that. The resolution implies that, and that is one of the reasons why it should be rejected.

I only put the question so that my hon. friend the Minister of Finance could have an opportunity of saying whether he intended that a minister of the Crown of Canada should question the good faith of a great and friendly nation like the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I certainly do not.

We in Ontario had no reason to complain of their good faith in so far as cattle, etc., are concerned. I do not think it is wise for a minister of the Crown, no matter what he may think, to question the good faith of a friendly nation.	.	>

speechtext:
Item agreed to.
113. Cocoanuts, desiccated, sweetened or not, per pound-British preferential, 3 cents; intermediate, 4 cents; general, 4 cents.
Is there any change in that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is a change rendered necessary by the action of last year in reference to the West Indian treaty. Previous to the negotiation of the West Indian treaty the rates were: British preferential, 3 cents; and general, 5 cents. On account of the West Indian theaty, and, in making the adjustment that was necessary in order to meet its provisions, we changed the rate to 3 cents British preferential, and 4 cents general tariff.
Immediately after the Budget was brought down last year, complaint was made by the manufacturers of dessicated cocoanut that the adjustment we had made was unfair to them and really prevented them from carrying on business in competition with the manufacturers of Ceylon. In Canada cocoanuts are bought in the West Indies. A bag of cocoanuts weighs 160 pounds and the freight has to be paid on that 160 pounds, while the product obtained from 160 pounds is only thirty-three pounds. The manufacturer in 'Ceylon who has cocoanuts at his own door, manufactures his desiccated cocoanut and ships it into -Canada without having to pay the freight for hundreds of miles on -cocoanuts, producing only one-fiftli of their weight dn product. I sent Mir. Russell to Montreal to inquire whether the complaint was well founded, and he reported it was, and in order to rectify what was an undoubted injustice to the cocoanut manufacturers of Canada, by reason of the changes which were rendered necessary by the W-est Indian treaty, we have had to propose this modification in the tariff and to increase the two -cents British preference to three cents, in order that our manufacturers may be in as good a position as they were before the negotiation of the West Indian treaty.
Has item 99a, evaporated bananas, anything to do with the West Indian treaty?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is intended to promote West Indian trade and to put this commodity the trade in which is increasing be-

tween the West Indies and ourselves, upon the same basis as currants and raisins.
Is the rate increased or decreased?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It will come in now free from the British West Indies. The value is about eight cents per pound and the former rate was-Brit'sh preference seventeen and one-half per cent; intermediate, twenty-two and one-quarter per cent; general, thirty-five per cent.
What is it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Jamaica Food Products Company wrote to say that they were importing evaporated bananas from Jamaica, which business was said to be increasing with prospects of an enormous trade being built up in it. They say the evaporated bananas cannot be manufactured in Canada, as the fruit requires to be ripened on the tree, allowing all the starch therein to be turned in to fruit sugar.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Amyl alcohol or refined fusil oil, when imported by the Department of Inland Revenue or by a person licensed by the Minister of Inland Revneue, to be denatured for use in the manufacture of metal varnishes or lacquers, to be entered at ports prescribed by regulations of the Ministers of Customs and Inland Revenue, subject to the Inland Revenue Act and to the regulations of the Department of Inland Revenue-British preferential, free; intermediate, free; general, free.
What is the explanation of this?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
With the restriction mentioned in 157-a, amyl alcohol or refined fusil oil is placed upon the free list. The reason for the change is to encourage the manufacture of metal lacquers in Canada.	The duty
on amyl alcohol, which cannot be procured in Canada, is $2.40 per gallon under the present tariff, while the varnish made therefrom is dutiable at about 60 cents per gallon. In other words, $2.40 would have to be paid upon the raw material by the manufacture of lacquer, and by reason of this condition metal varnishes or lacquers cannot be made in Canada. An American firm has embarked upon the business of manufacturing metal varnishes or lacquers -in the town of Port Hops.	They
were unaware, not having been advised, that this duty of $2.40 existed, and having
APRIn 29, 1914
got their plant installed and being ready to manufacture, they found they would have to pay this duty. I need not say to you that the good town of Port Hope *was sorely disturbed about the matter, and upon representations having been made we brought down this tariff change which makes amyl alcohol or refined fusil oil, free, with the limitation mentioned in the item. A license of $50 a year will have to be paid by the parties importing and using this amyl alcohol, and 50 cents a gallon excise will have to be paid, and they will also have to pay for the time of the Inland Revenue officers in making the necessary inspection.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Provided that on the goods specified in item 178 and imported hy mail on and after first day of July, 1914, duties may be paid by Customs Revenue stamps, under regulations by the Minister of Customs, at the rates specified in said item, except that on each separate package weighing not more than one ounce the duty
shall be	each-British preferential, 1 cent',
intermediate, 1 cent; general, 1 cent.
What is referred to here ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Item 178 of the Customs tariff relates to advertising and printed matter. A great deal of that matter comes in from outside, being sent in by firms desiring to advertise in Canada, not necessarily consigned to any party purchasing it, aDd it is dutiable under the provisions of item 178. When sent in in envelopes it is held at the frontier and the party has to be communicated with in order that the duty may be paid upon advertising matter which may weigh an ounce or two only. The Commissioner of Customs has suggested that the difficulties which have arisen under the present system can be met by the proviso in this item that Customs revenue stamps may be used, with the exception mentioned, namely, that on each separate package weighing not more than one ounce, the duty shall not be more than one cent, a cent being the smallest coin we mint. As the rate is fifteen cents a pound under item 178, and as there are sixteen ounces to the pound, a cent will be charged for the ounce and stamps may be used.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
184. Newspapers, and quarterly, monthly, and semi-monthly magazines, and weekly literary papers, unbound; tailors', milliners' and mantle-makers' fashion plates when imported m single copies in sheet form with magazines or periodical trade journals-British preferential, free; intermediate, free ; general, free.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am told that it was the original intention of the tariff of 1907 to provide that only single copies of fashion plates should come in free; but the item has been abused, and fashion plates are being ordered abroad and being brought in free of duty under this item. The intention of the amendment is to provide that single copies only shall be brought in with these newspapers and magazines. The result will be that these fashion plates will now be lithographed and printed in Canada instead of abroad.
What was the duty before?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It was all under item 178- 15 cents per pound.
What is to be the tariff on fashion plates hereafter?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That will fall under item 178-15 cents per pound.
Were magazines and newspapers dutiable before?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Magazines were not. The item is modified. If my hon. friend will look at item 184 in the tariff as it is now, he will observe that it stops short at the words ' fashion plates.' Under the change mat I have made that item disappears, and item 184, as it appears in the tariff resolution, is inserted.
Is not there any post office regulation prohibiting fashion plates coming through the mails in a periodical journal of any kind? Why would they come in single copies with journals?
As supplements.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They are continually being sent in that way. The Ladies' Home Journal and other journals may have fashion plates enclosed. Some of the larger departmental .stares have been giving their orders for fashion plates and for some of their advertising matter abroad, and bringing them in under this item free of duty. We think that business might fairly be reserved under a protective tariff to the printers and lithographers of Canada. It has been a very much discussed question; and I have on record here a number of letters from engraving companies stating that this matter has been under consideration for a long time and that it is of very great importance to the trade.
There is a duty on catalogues, is there not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Ten and fifteen cents per pound.
Do you propose to maintain that duty?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
188a. Decalcomania paper not printed when imported by manufacturers of decalcomania transfers to be used in their own factories in the manufacture of decalcomania transfers- British preferential, free; intermediate, free; general, free.
Tell us the meaning of that first word, and we will let the item go through.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not wonder at my hon. friend's asking that question. That word puzzled me for some little time. The decalcomania paper is used in making decalcomania transfers. There is a process of transferring prints from paper and making them adhere to glass, porcelain and other articles. Decalcomonia transfers are chiefly used for advertising purposes.
Is it of advantage to the paper-makers?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not to my knowledge. These people get in the decalcomania paper, which is not made in Canada, free under this item. They can put on their aluminum letters and transfer them to glass, porcelain and other articles.

Item agreed to.
208. Boracic acid and borax in packages of not less than twenty-five pounds weight; hydro-fluosilicic acid; oxalic acid ; tannic acid; ammonia, sulphate of; sal ammoniac and nitrate of ammonia; cyanide of potassium; cyanide of sodium and cyanogen bromide for reducing metals in mining operations; antimony salts, viz.:-tartar emetic, chlorine and lactate (anto-monine) ; arsenous oxide; oxide of cobalt; oxide of tin; bichloride of tin; tin crystals; oxide of copper; precipitate of copper, crude; sulphate of copper (blue vitriol) ; verdigris or subacetate of copper, dry; sulphate of iron (copperas) ; sulphate of zinc; chloride of zine; sulphur and brimstone, crude or in roll or flour; cream of tartar, in crystals or argols; tartaric acid crystals ; iodine, crude; bromide; phosphorus; sulphide of arsenic; carbon bisulphide-British preferential, free; intermediate, free; general, free.
What is the change in this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I would call attention to item 208a-chloride of lime and hypochlorite of lime. We have taken out of this item 208a of the tariff, chloride of lime and

hypochlorite of lime, and we have inserted in it carbon .bisulphide. Item 208 of the present tariff is repealed, and the new item 208 takes its place. We have placed carbon. bisulphide on the free list because it is an article used in exterminating fruit and grain pests. We have been requested by the British Columbia Government through its Minister of Agriculture to place carbon bisulphide upon the free list.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
208a. Chloride of lime and hypochlorite of lime

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
1.	When in packages of not less than twenty-five pounds weight each, per one hundred pounds-British preferential, 10 cents; intermediate, 15 cents ; general, 15 cmts.
2.	When in packages of less than twenty-five pounds in weight each-British preferential, 171 per cent; intermediate, 25 per cent; general, 25 per cent.
Why is chloride of lime subject to a duty when it was not subject before?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If my hon. friend will look at item 210 and take up the two items together, I think I can more intelligently explain the matter. There is at Windsor, Ont., a salt plant, and there are, as my hon. friends know, deposits of salt in several parts of Ontario. The Windsor plant has at the present time a capacity of 4,000,000 pounds of caustic soda. This company have had no duty upon caustic soda which is one of the products of salt manufacture; nor have they had any duty upon chloride of lime or upon hypochlorite of lime, which are by-products on caustic soda production. They have been making application for a considerable time for a reasonable tariff in respect of these two articles. They have set forth the view that they could double their plant and their output and supply ail the caustic soda, chloride of lime and hypo-chloride of lime required in Canada with a reasonable protection.
Without increasing the price, I hope.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I hope so. Sometimes our hopes are not realized, I know. But I think that in time, with an increased output, there would be no substantial increase in the price. The committee will observe that the rates are specific, and they amount to about eleven per cent British preferential and sixteen and one-half per cent general tariff. The differentiation is shown in the items of the tariff as follows:

Caustic soda:
1.	When in packages of not less than twenty-five pounds weight; free.
2.	When in packages of less than twenty-five pounds weight; British preferential, 10 per cent; intermediate, 12i per cent; general, 15 per cent
These are on the free list when in packages of not less than twenty-five pounds. But when in packages of less than twenty-five pounds, the duty under the British preferential is ten per cent and under the general tariff fifteen per cent; now to be increased to seventeen and one-half and twenty-five per cent. The consumption in Canada is about 16,000,000 pounds and the material is used by soap manufacturers, cotton manufacturers-for bleaching purposes; chloride of lime, as hon. members know, is commercially known as ' bleaching powder '*-by pulp and paper manufacturers and other industries. But these will not be affected to any serious extent.

Does the hon. minister
mean to say that these people in Windsor will not put up the price? They would be crazy if they did not; there would be no use in protecting them from competition if they are to go on selling at the price of competition. This caustic soda is used largely by soap manufacturers. They buy it by the carload. So, while the duty is small-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
About 3 cents per 100 pound of soap.
Mr. NESBITT;-yet because of the large quantities used, this change will make quite a difference in the cost of the raw material. While I have nothing to say against my hon. friend from Essex, and do not wish to prevent this factory succeeding, I hardly think the benefit of the community from this industry will be sufficient to offset the increase in price of the material. These people have increased their price of salt in the last four or five years quite sufficiently to make a profit without protecting them on chloride of lime and caustic soda. The barrel of salt that we used to get for 90 cents we are now paying $1.55 for.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Of course, the hon. gentleman is quite right; the tendency will be to increase the price. But I would not say that the price would be permanently increased, and I hope not. But discussing a similar question last night in connection with structural steel, I said that no doubt the price would be higher-otherwise, as the hon. gentleman said, there would be
no use in imposing the duty. But this is not to raise the price necessarily, but to give the benefit of the market to the home manufacturer. There is no use in blinking the fact that we may look for a slight increase in price. Some representations have been made to me on behalf of those affected, 'but generally they look at it in a fair-minded way. The soap-makers say: We have, speaking generally, a protection of 15 to 35 per cent, and we can hardly deny the caustic soda and bleaching powder manufacturer a reasonable protection on his product. For the most part, I have been surprised at the fair-mindedness they have exhibited with regard- to this proposed change, against which, of course, they cannot urge any objection on principle.
Is the industry worth having?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No doubt. If I were to
give the floor to my hon. friend from North Essex (Mr. Wilcox), I have no doubt he could talk for an hour on that subject.

Do not do it.
Mr. WILCOX; Let the item pass or Tj will.
Carried.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The number of employees at present in the chemical plant is sixty-five and the value of that plant $750,000. Steps have been taken already to duplicate that plant in view of this tariff change.
Is this not a byproduct of salt? And in giving the number of employees, does not that include those engaged in the production of sailt?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, these are in the chemical plant. I cannot put the doctrine of reasonable protection on a higher basis than to say that we get the manufacturers here if we have it and we do not get them if we do not have it.

But it is of very questionable value to the country, particularly where there is only one industry.
Mr. NESBITT; While I agree with the Minister of Finance in many respects, he must bear in mind that in the salt business they have a great number of men already employed, whereas this industry, even if doubled will only mean from 120 to 130

employees, and labourers at that-not experts by any manner or means.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There are other establishments; there are large salt deposits in Ontario, as the hon. gentleman knows.

Of course there are, and *what I say is that they .should be able to make enough money out of the increased price of salt to be able to do without this protection on their by-products. There is no doubt that there is an arrangement among the salt people as to prices. Everybody knows that. You can no more break a price than you could if the industry were in the hands of one man. Therefore, I am not strongly in favour of putting on duty for that sort of people when, as the minister no doubt knows, there is an arrangement among them as to price.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The principle is the same.
Why is there a difference in the duty on chloride of lime in packages of different sizes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I cannot give that information off-hand. I will try to get it for my hon. friend to-morrow.
296. Flint, ground flint stones, felspar, fluorspar, magnesite, mica schist, cliff, chalk, china or Cornwall stone, ground or unground, refuse stone, not sawn, hammered or chiselled nor fit for flagstones, building stone or paving- British preferential, free; intermediate, free; general, free.
Were the articles enumerated in this item previously on the dutiable list? If so, what is the change?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mica schist is admitted
free of duty under the present tariff. There has been some doubt in the minds of the customs officials as to whether under the existing tariff it should be admitted free, and we have decided, in order to clear the matter up, to put mica schist upon the free list. The change proposed in this item will make talc or soapstone dutiable under item 711 at fifteen per cent British preferential,

seventeen and one-half intermediate and seventeen and one-half general. In other words, talc or soapstone, which was formerly on the free list, is now dutiable at seventeen and one-half per cent general tariff. I may say that this article may be obtained in unlimited quantities in the county of Hastings, Ontario.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Progress reported.
